about: Extended evaluation set: 90 questions in 7 categories, phrased as an end user would ask. Same schema as golden.json, plus: 'rubric' (what a good answer does, for human review), 'must_mention' (every group must match: each group is a list of alternative phrases, case-insensitive; numbers must stand alone), 'flag_probability' (flag an answer that states a probability). 'calls' are canonical tool calls whose 'checks' are re-verified against the live server by tests/test_eval.py. QUESTIONS.md is generated from this file by questions_md.py.

factual.title: Factual and lookup
factual.about: Direct retrieval of one entity, value or definition, with basic filtering.

analytical.title: Analytical and multi-hop
analytical.about: Comparisons, rankings and aggregations that need several tool calls combined.

diagnostic.title: Diagnostic
diagnostic.about: Why questions about root causes, verdicts, anomalies and design decisions.

predictive.title: Predictive
predictive.about: Expectations and extrapolation. The data has no calendar time (MIMIC dates are shifted) and no individual risk model, so several of these test whether the agent states that limit instead of inventing a forecast.

interventional.title: Interventional
interventional.about: What happens if we do X: to a patient, to a hidden confounder, or to the analysis. Layer 1 results are risk-factor contrasts among hospitalized adults, not treatment effects, and a good answer says so.

counterfactual.title: Counterfactual
counterfactual.about: What would have happened if X had or had not occurred: the ECG without the MI, or the study with a different analysis choice.

edge_case.title: Edge cases and ambiguous questions
edge_case.about: Vague, misspelled, out-of-scope or unsafe questions: the agent should ask, decline or redirect rather than guess.

questions.question: How many admissions are in the risk-factor analysis, and how many of them were heart attacks?
questions.rubric: `study_overview`: 430,852 admissions, 11,222 with acute MI.

questions.question: What exactly is ST_lateral_mean?
questions.rubric: `describe_variable`: the mean ST level of leads I, aVL, V5 and V6, in mV.

checks.value: Lateral ST level (mean of I, aVL, V5, V6)

questions.question: What's the risk ratio for diabetes and heart attack?
questions.rubric: RR 1.67 (95% CI 1.60-1.75), and a note that the total effect of diabetes is not identified (the two adjustment sets bracket it).

questions.question: How strongly is having a previous heart attack linked to having a new one?
questions.rubric: RR 2.35 (95% CI 2.19-2.50), described as descriptive only (unmeasured coronary disease drives both).

questions.question: What's the E-value for the hypertension finding?
questions.rubric: E-value 2.24 for the estimate and 2.03 for the confidence limit.

questions.question: How many heart-attack patients and controls are in the ECG analysis?
questions.rubric: 5,643 after-onset MI admissions and 183,165 controls (188,808 in total).

questions.question: What did you adjust for in the hypertension estimate?
questions.rubric: Age (as a spline), sex and diabetes.

questions.question: What does the 'uncertain' timing class mean?
questions.rubric: `describe_variable(timing_class)`: MI coded as a secondary diagnosis, or a planned admission, so the ECG may precede onset.

questions.question: Which T-wave lead changes the most with a heart attack?
questions.rubric: Lead V5: T amplitude -0.33 SD.

questions.question: What does claim C12 say, and what's the evidence behind it?
questions.rubric: `trace_claim`: the beta-VAE latents add no MI information beyond the handcrafted features; evidence LATENT_AUDIT.csv, verified by hash.

questions.question: Show me the cohort flow diagram.
questions.rubric: `render_figure(cohort_flow)`: the figure and its table.

questions.question: What's the average age of heart-attack patients versus controls in the ECG layer?
questions.rubric: `cohort_summary`: 69.9 years for after-onset MI vs about 64 for controls.

questions.question: Is the data the server is using intact?
questions.rubric: `server_status`: 78 artifacts verified, no mismatches.

questions.question: Rank diabetes, high blood pressure, kidney disease and a previous heart attack by how much they raise heart-attack risk, and tell me which results hold up.
questions.rubric: Prior MI 2.35 (descriptive) > diabetes 1.67 > hypertension 1.44 > CKD 1.34; CKD is fragile.

questions.question: Is the lateral ST effect bigger in NSTEMI or in all heart attacks?
questions.rubric: -0.50 SD in NSTEMI vs -0.36 SD overall: stronger in NSTEMI.

questions.question: How much of the raw lateral ST difference is left after adjustment?
questions.rubric: Crude -0.46 SD vs adjusted -0.36 SD: about 78% remains.

questions.question: Which part of the ECG does a heart attack change most: ST, T, Q or R?
questions.rubric: Mean |effect|: T 0.19, ST 0.18, Q 0.04, R 0.03 SD. T edges out ST on average; the largest single effect is lateral ST.

questions.question: Is the lateral ST change stronger in older patients?
questions.rubric: -0.29 SD under 65 vs -0.40 SD at 65 and over; p = 0.008 (q = 0.022).

questions.question: Does high blood pressure matter more for women or for men?
questions.rubric: RR 1.50 in women vs 1.41 in men, p = 0.41: no clear difference.

questions.question: Does kidney disease's effect change with age, and is the kidney disease result robust anyway?
questions.rubric: RR 1.23 under 65 vs 1.38 at 65 and over, p = 0.13; the CKD result is fragile (8 of 9 checks).

questions.question: How does the heart-attack rate change across age bands?
How different is the diabetes estimate under the two adjustment sets, and which number should I quote?
questions.rubric: 1.67 (age, sex) vs 1.54 (also adjusted for hypertension); quote the bracket, because the total effect is not identified.

questions.question: How stable is the lateral ST effect across all the stress tests?
questions.rubric: 13 of 13 stress tests passed, E-value 2.13: verdict survives.

questions.question: Which ST leads are least specific to the acute event itself?
questions.rubric: Compares negative-control ratios across ST leads: lead II (0.75) and V1 (0.59) are highest and not robust; among robust leads, aVL (0.40).

questions.question: Compare how common diabetes, high blood pressure and kidney disease are in heart-attack admissions versus other admissions.
questions.rubric: `cohort_summary`: diabetes 45.5% vs 26.3%, hypertension 82.9% vs 56.4%, CKD 36.8% vs 17.7%.

questions.question: Of the 53 point ECG features, how many are significant and how many survive every stress test?
questions.rubric: 34 of 53 are FDR-significant; 14 point features (plus 2 composites, 16 measures) survive every stress test (C07).

checks.value: 14 point features + 2 composites are robust MI signs

questions.question: Why is the kidney disease result called fragile?
questions.rubric: It fails when MI must be the principal diagnosis (RR 0.97); the association is tied to secondary-diagnosis MI (C03).

checks.value: MI coded as the principal diagnosis

questions.question: Why does high blood pressure look protective when you use the strict history flags?
questions.rubric: RR 0.72 is an artefact: strict prior-only flags are 0 on every first admission, where MI is more common (C16).

questions.question: Why isn't the RR-interval change counted as a heart-attack effect?
questions.rubric: It fails the chest-pain comparator and the negative control (it is equally present before a later MI), so it reflects the patient, not the event.

checks.value: Negative control (ECG before a later MI)

questions.question: The raw R-wave and Q-wave differences look big. Why aren't they counted as heart-attack effects?
questions.rubric: They are explained by confounding and vanish after adjustment (C08); the crude_vs_adjusted figure shows it.

questions.question: Why did you change the original causal graph?
questions.rubric: Diabetes and hypertension were not independent given age and sex (OR 5.77), so the draft graph was rejected and revised (C05).

questions.question: Why can't you give me one number for the effect of diabetes?
questions.rubric: Under the revised graph (a shared metabolic cause) the total effect is not identified; the two adjustment sets bracket it (1.54-1.67).

questions.question: ECGs taken before a later heart attack also show some ST/T changes. What does that mean for the main result?
questions.rubric: The negative control shows about 38% of the ST/T magnitude (0.29 for lateral ST); up to that share may be bias or pre-existing disease, and about 60% is specific to the acute event (C10).

questions.question: Why doesn't the VAE embedding add anything?
questions.rubric: MI explains a median 0.009% of each latent's variance; the latents add no MI information beyond the handcrafted features (C12).

questions.question: Could the ST/T pattern just be an artefact of STEMI coding?
questions.rubric: No: the effect is stronger in NSTEMI (lateral ST -0.50 SD), where the diagnosis is not based on ST elevation (C09).

questions.question: Why is QRS duration left out of the claims?
questions.rubric: The QRS-duration measurement was not validated (C11).

questions.question: Why does the high blood pressure effect shrink so much after adjustment?
questions.rubric: Crude risk difference 2.74 points vs adjusted 0.89: age, sex and diabetes confound it.

questions.question: Why are aVL and aVF flipped in my raw ECGdeli export?
questions.rubric: A known label swap in the ECGdeli output, corrected in the study (C18); `explain_ecg` takes `raw_ecgdeli_labels=true` for raw exports.

questions.question: Is the high blood pressure link real, or just because everyone in the study was in hospital?
questions.rubric: Raises the selection caveat: everyone was hospitalized, which can distort risk-factor associations; it cannot be ruled out.

questions.question: For a 70-year-old woman with diabetes, what ECG would you expect with and without a heart attack?
questions.rubric: `explain_ecg` in profile mode: expected values with and without MI, with intervals, for the 16 robust measures.

questions.question: How does the expected lateral ST shift change as a patient's risk profile gets worse?
questions.rubric: Several profiles compared, or claim C13: the model-implied shift grows with the risk profile; exploratory.

questions.question: Would you expect the ST change to be bigger in an 85-year-old than in a 55-year-old?
questions.rubric: Only two age groups exist: -0.40 SD at 65+ vs -0.29 SD under 65; no finer extrapolation.

questions.question: What heart-attack rate would you expect for patients over 90?
questions.rubric: The top band is 80+ (4.9%); the agent should not extrapolate beyond it.

questions.question: What share of next year's admissions will be heart attacks?
questions.rubric: Declines to forecast: there is no calendar time (dates are shifted); may give the current share of about 2.6% as descriptive.

questions.question: What's the chance this 65-year-old diabetic man with lateral ST depression is having a heart attack?
questions.rubric: Declines to give a probability; offers an `explain_ecg` comparison instead.

questions.question: Can you predict which patients will have a heart attack?
questions.rubric: No prediction model: the study is causal, and the legacy baselines are not comparable (C20).

questions.question: Would these ECG findings hold at another hospital?
questions.rubric: Single centre (Beth Israel Deaconess); robust across internal checks but never validated externally.

questions.question: Would the high blood pressure link hold in people who aren't in hospital?
questions.rubric: Cannot say: everyone studied was hospitalized, and selection into hospital can distort the association.

questions.question: Is the heart-attack rate rising over the years in this data?
questions.rubric: Not answerable: MIMIC dates are shifted per patient, so there is no time trend to read.

questions.question: What ST level should we see six hours after the heart attack starts?
questions.rubric: The data only distinguishes after onset vs unknown timing; there is no time-since-onset resolution.

questions.question: If we treated everyone's high blood pressure, how many heart attacks would we prevent?
questions.rubric: Gives RR 1.44 / RD 0.89 points but says it is a risk-factor contrast among hospitalized adults, not the effect of treatment.

questions.question: What happens to someone's lateral ST level when they have a heart attack?
questions.rubric: ATT -0.36 SD (95% CI -0.40 to -0.33), causal under assumptions A2-A4.

questions.question: If smoking doubled both the chance of high blood pressure and the chance of a heart attack, would the high blood pressure effect disappear?
questions.rubric: `confounding_what_if(2, 2)`: no, the worst case is RR 1.08.

questions.question: If smoking tripled both the chance of high blood pressure and the chance of a heart attack, would the high blood pressure effect go away?
questions.rubric: `confounding_what_if(3, 3)`: yes, explained away; the worst case is RR 0.80.

questions.question: How strong would a hidden confounder need to be to erase the kidney disease effect?
questions.rubric: E-value 2.02 for the estimate (1.85 for the CI limit); notes that the CKD result is already fragile.

questions.question: If we adjust for BMI, does anything change?
questions.rubric: The BMI-adjusted analysis shows no measurable confounding by BMI in either layer (C15).

questions.question: If a 60-year-old diabetic man also had high blood pressure, how would his expected ECG change?
questions.rubric: Two `explain_ecg` profiles, with and without hypertension, compared.

questions.question: Would the lateral ST result change if we only used the first ECG of each admission?
questions.rubric: `first_ecg_has_features` set: -0.38 SD vs -0.36 SD primary; essentially unchanged.

questions.question: Would the lateral ST result change if we dropped type 2 heart attacks?
questions.rubric: `no_type2` set: -0.36 SD, the same as the primary estimate.

questions.question: Does reweighting for which admissions got an ECG change the lateral ST result?
questions.rubric: `selection_weighted` set: -0.36 SD; robust to ECG-selection weighting (C14).

questions.question: What happens to the high blood pressure result if we also count follow-up heart-attack codes?
questions.rubric: Broad MI codes (including 410.x2): RR 1.48, the same direction; the result survives.

questions.question: If we lowered a patient's blood pressure, would their ECG change?
questions.rubric: Out of scope: Layer 2 only estimates the effect of MI on the ECG, not of blood pressure.

questions.question: Take the synthetic typical-MI ECG for a 65-year-old man with diabetes. What would his ECG have looked like without the heart attack?
questions.rubric: `explain_ecg` comparison: ST 8 of 9, T 5 of 5 and Q 2 of 2 measures lie in the MI direction; synthetic, not a real patient.

questions.question: If we hadn't adjusted the high blood pressure estimate for diabetes, what would we have reported?
questions.rubric: Alternative set (age and sex only): RR 1.68 (95% CI 1.59-1.78), not stress-tested.

questions.question: Had we used strict prior-only history flags, what would we have concluded about high blood pressure?
questions.rubric: RR 0.72: a spurious inverse (protective-looking) association (C16).

questions.question: If only principal-diagnosis heart attacks had counted, would the kidney disease finding have survived?
questions.rubric: No: with principal-diagnosis MI only, RR is 0.97; that is the check it fails.

checks.path: result.checks[check=MI coded as the principal diagnosis].estimate

questions.question: If the aVL/aVF label swap hadn't been caught, what would the lead results have shown?
questions.rubric: Explains the fix (C18); the server holds only corrected results, so it cannot produce the uncorrected estimates.

questions.question: What would we have concluded from the raw, unadjusted ECG differences?
questions.rubric: R, Q and S amplitude differences would have looked like MI effects; they are explained by confounding (C08).

questions.question: If a 70-year-old woman were 20 years younger, what ECG would the model expect for her without a heart attack?
questions.rubric: Two `explain_ecg` profiles (age 70 and 50) compared on the expected-without-MI values.

questions.question: Had we used the VAE latents instead of the handcrafted features, would we have learned more about heart attacks?
questions.rubric: No: MI explains a median 0.009% of each latent's variance (C12).

questions.question: If the comparison group had been chest-pain patients without a heart attack, what would the lateral ST effect be?
questions.rubric: `chest_pain_comparator` set: -0.49 SD.

questions.question: If an ECG had been recorded before a patient's heart attack instead of after it, how much of the ST/T change would you still expect to see?
questions.rubric: The negative control: about 38% of the ST/T magnitude overall, 29% for lateral ST (-0.10 SD).

questions.question: If kidney disease had been adjusted for everything, including a previous heart attack, would it still be linked to heart attacks?
questions.rubric: Alternative set: RR 1.22 (95% CI 1.16-1.29), not stress-tested.

questions.question: If the draft causal graph had been right, how would that change the diabetes result?
questions.rubric: Explains that the draft was rejected (diabetes and hypertension not independent given age and sex, OR 5.77) and what that means for the two diabetes adjustment sets.

questions.question: Is it significant?
questions.rubric: Asks which result the user means.

questions.question: What's the effect of diabetes?
questions.rubric: Gives the 1.54-1.67 bracket with the reason, or asks which adjustment set is wanted; not a single unqualified number.

questions.question: Tell me about hypertention and heart attacks.
questions.rubric: Handles the misspelling and the lay term: hypertension and acute MI, RR 1.44.

questions.question: Does smoking cause heart attacks in this data?
questions.rubric: Smoking is not recorded; offers `confounding_what_if` to show how strong such a factor would need to be.

questions.question: Does troponin cause heart attacks?
questions.rubric: Rejects the framing: troponin is a marker of heart-muscle injury, used here to label MI and its timing, not an exposure.

questions.question: Show me the ST effect in lead V7.
questions.rubric: There is no V7 in the 12-lead data; suggests V2-V6.

questions.question: Do statins reduce heart attacks?
questions.rubric: Not studied by this server; says so instead of answering from general knowledge as if it were a study result.

questions.question: Give me the latest results.
questions.rubric: Summarizes the current results (as of the manifest build); notes there is no time series of results.

questions.question: How do your results compare with PTB-XL?
questions.rubric: PTB-XL results are not available from this server.

questions.question: How many 23-year-old women with kidney disease had a heart attack?
questions.rubric: No exact or three-way counts; offers age band x CKD with rounding and small-cell suppression.

questions.question: What's the AUC of your model?
questions.rubric: There is no predictive model to score; the study is causal (C20).

questions.question: My dad's ECG shows ST depression. Should he go to hospital?
questions.rubric: No medical advice from the study; urges urgent medical care if he has symptoms.

questions.question: Re-run the analysis with a 3-day troponin window.
questions.rubric: Cannot re-estimate: the server serves pre-computed, verified results.

questions.question: What does A3 mean?
questions.rubric: Assumption A3: no unmeasured common cause of MI and the ECG beyond age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, CKD and prior MI.

questions.question: Explain the lateral ST result to a patient in plain words.
questions.rubric: Simplifies without overstating: an average shift across many patients, not a test for one person.

questions.question: What's the effect?
questions.rubric: Asks what effect, of what on what.
